en: The Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya: The Bhikṣu Precept Manual, translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhabhadra of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty; Chapter Six:
The Dharma of the Six Mindfulnesses.
"First, one should know the number of days: the first day, the second day, and so on up to the fourteenth and fifteenth days; one must fully understand whether the month is large or small."
"Second, at dawn one should perform the rite of giving food:
'Today I obtain food to give to such-and-such a person; that person has no expectations toward me, and I shall eat it.'"
Thus he spoke three times. "Third, one should daily recall the number of years since one's full ordination.
Fourth, one should mindfully recollect and maintain awareness of the robes received and those offered through pure giving."
"Fifth, one should be mindful not to eat separately from the assembly.
Sixth, one should be mindful whether one is ill or not.
From the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya Prātimokṣa Bhikṣu-śīla-mūla*: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
One month of winter has passed, lacking one night; there remains but one night and three months until old age and death draw near, and the Buddha-dharma is about to perish.
Venerable sirs!
For the sake of attaining the Way, one should apply oneself with single-minded diligence and vigor. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of single-minded diligence and vigor; how much more so for the other factors conducive to enlightenment!
“The one who has not yet received full ordination has already departed.
Now that the Saṃgha is in harmony, what should be done first?
One person replied:
“The Uposatha and the recitation of the Prātimokṣa. “Venerable sirs!
The bhikṣus who have not come shall announce their *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi*.”
“Who has received the *chanda* (consent) from the bhikṣuṇīs?
“With palms joined like ten fingers, I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas;
now that I am about to recite the precepts, may the Saṃgha listen with a single mind.”
Even regarding minor offenses, one’s mind should feel great dread;
having committed a fault, repent with single-mindedness, and never commit it again.
The horse of the mind gallops down evil paths; when abandoned to heedlessness, it is difficult to restrain.
The Buddha has taught all the precepts and practices, just like sharp reins and bits.
When the Buddha’s mouth utters his instructions, the virtuous are able to believe and accept them;
such a person is a well-tamed horse, capable of destroying the army of afflictions.
If one does not accept instruction, nor takes delight in the precepts,
such a person is like an untamed horse, submerged in the army of afflictions.
If a person guards the precepts as a gayal ox cherishes its tail;
Binding the mind with heedfulness, like a monkey bound by chains,
one should always be diligent day and night for the sake of seeking true wisdom;
such a person, within the Buddha-dharma, is able to attain a pure livelihood.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today is the fifteenth day for the poṣadha and the recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha with one mind perform the poṣadha together and recite the Prātimokṣa."
Thus it was announced:
"Venerable sirs!
Now, for the Poṣadha ceremony, the Prātimokṣa shall be recited; may the Saṃgha listen with a single mind."
Those who have committed an offense should confess it; those who are free from offense should remain silent. By remaining silent, it should be known that the Venerable Ones are pure.
As each bhikṣu asks and answers, this procedure is proclaimed three times within the assembly of bhikṣus.

If a bhikṣu, when thus proclaimed three times in the midst of the bhikṣu-saṃgha, remembers having committed an offense, he should confess it; if he does not confess it, he incurs the offense of intentional lying.
Venerable sirs!

Therefore, the Buddha has declared that the offense of lying is a dharma that obstructs the Path. For this reason, a bhikṣu who seeks purity should, mindful of his transgression, confess it; by confessing, he finds peace and security, whereas by not confessing, his offense becomes increasingly grave.
“Venerable sirs!
The introduction to the Prātimokṣa has been recited.
Now I ask the venerable sirs:”
Is there purity in this?
Is there purity in this?
Is there purity in this?
“Venerable sirs!
Since there is silence, you are pure in this matter; thus shall this be held.
Venerable sirs!”
These are the four *pārājika* rules, which are recited every half-month during the *Prātimokṣa*.

"If a bhikṣu has received full ordination within a harmonious Saṃgha, and without returning his vows or relinquishing them due to weakness of resolve, engages in sexual intercourse—even with an animal—this bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense and may not dwell in communion."

"The Buddha was staying in the city of Vaiśālī; five years after his enlightenment, during the fifth fortnight of the winter season on the twelfth day, after the meal, sitting facing east when one and a half shadows remained, he established this precept for the Elder Yaśa Kākaṇḍakaputra."
"Once a rule has been established, one should practice in accordance with it; this is called 'conformity with the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu, in a village or in an open space, takes what is not given—theft of another's property—and the king or his officials arrest him, execute him, bind him, or banish him, saying: 'Ho, man!'"
"You are a thief!
You are foolish!
If a bhikṣu takes what is not given in this manner, that bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.

The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha; it was the tenth day of the second fortnight of the winter season in the sixth year since his enlightenment. After his meal, he sat facing east when the shadow was two and a half *vitasti* long, and for the sake of the elder Ghaṭīkāra, the potter’s son, and on account of King Bimbisāra and the *pāṃśukūlika* (rag-robe) bhikṣus, he established this precept.
Once it has been prescribed, one should practice in accordance with it; this is called "conformity with the Dharma.
"If a bhikṣu, with his own hand, takes the life of a human being, or seeks out and provides a knife to a killer, or instructs another to die, or praises death, saying: 'Ho!'"
"What is the use of living a life of evil?
Death is better than life.

Forming such a thought and such a conception, he uses skillful means to praise the joy of death, and because of this—no other reason—he dies, that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and is not to live in communion.

The Buddha was staying in the city of Vaiśālī; it was the ninth day of the third fortnight of the winter season in the sixth year since his enlightenment. Before the meal, while sitting facing north when the shadow was one and a half *vitasti* long, he established this precept for the sake of many monks who were tending to the sick, due to the incident involving the non-Buddhist Mṛgaśiras.
"Once a rule has been established, one should practice in accordance with it; this is called 'conformity to the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu, not having known or seen, claims to have attained superhuman noble dharmas and superior knowledge and vision, saying:
'I know thus; I see thus.'"
At a later time, whether he has been examined or not, having committed an offense, he desires to seek purification and thus speaks these words:
"Venerable sir!
I spoke what I did not know as if I knew it, and I spoke what I had not seen as if I saw it; my words were false and untrue."
“Excepting one who acts out of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), this bhikṣu commits a *pārājika* offense and is not to live in communion.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; in the sixth year after his enlightenment, on the thirteenth day of the fourth half-month of winter, after the meal and facing east when the shadow was three persons and a half, he established this precept for the many bhikṣus in the village and for the bhikṣus of overweening pride.
"Once they have been prescribed, one should practice in accordance with them;
this is called the 'Dharma of Conformity. Venerable sirs!
The four *pārājika* rules have now been recited."
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Is there purity in this matter?
Is there purity in this matter?
"Are you pure in this matter? "Venerable sirs!
We are pure in this matter, for we are silent; thus shall this matter be held."
The four matters concluded: "Venerable sirs!
These thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa dharmas are recited in turn every half-month as part of the Prātimokṣa."
"If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, except during a dream, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.

If a bhikṣu, with a mind transformed by lustful desire, engages in physical contact with a woman—whether grasping her hand, grasping her hair, or touching other parts of her body—and experiences pleasure from that contact, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"If a bhikṣu, with a mind transformed by lustful desire, speaks lewd words to a woman in accordance with the ways of sexual desire, as young men and women do, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"If a bhikṣu, with a mind transformed by lust, in the presence of a woman, extols his own person as an offering: 'Sister!
As for me, a śramaṇa who maintains pure precepts, practices wholesome dharmas, and cultivates the holy life, the offering of sexual intercourse is the foremost.'"

Saṃghāvaśeṣa. “If a bhikṣu, acting as a messenger, brings about the union of a man and a woman—whether it be for taking a wife or for illicit intercourse—even if only for a moment, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.”
"If a bhikṣu should beg for materials to build a hut for himself when there is no donor, it must be built according to the prescribed measurements:
twelve Sugata-spans in length and seven spans in width."
One should show the various bhikṣus the site for building a hut—a site that is free from difficulties and not obstructive.

If one personally solicits materials to build a hut on a site that is difficult or obstructive, for oneself and without an owner, and fails to show the various bhikṣus the site for building the hut, yet builds it in excess of the prescribed dimensions, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling for himself that has an owner, he should, having invited other bhikṣus, designate a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions."
If it is a difficult location or an obstructed location, or if it belongs to another for their own use, and if he does not point out the location to the other bhikṣus, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and resentment, slanders a pure and innocent bhikṣu with a groundless *pārājika* offense, desiring to destroy that bhikṣu’s pure conduct."
If, at a later time, whether he is investigated or not, he says:
"This matter was groundless; I spoke it because I was dwelling in anger and resentment," it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and resentment, because he is displeased, should defame another with a *pārājika* offense for a minor matter belonging to a different category that is not a *pārājika*, desiring to ruin that bhikṣu’s holy life (*brahmacarya*)."
Later, whether he is examined or not, he will say:
"I spoke out of anger over a minor matter of a different category."
Saṃghāvaśeṣa.
“If a bhikṣu, for the sake of breaking up a harmonious Saṃgha, diligently employs skillful means and persists in the matter of causing schism, engaging in contention.”
The monks should admonish him, saying: "Venerable one!
Do not strive with skillful means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, nor persist in disputes over matters that cause a schism; you should act in harmony with the Saṃgha."

Why is this? Because the Saṃgha is harmonious, joyful, and free from dispute; they train together as one, like water and milk blending, illuminating through the Dharma as it is taught, and dwelling in peace and happiness.
If he relinquishes it when admonished in this manner, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, he should be admonished a second and third time. If he relinquishes that matter, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"If a bhikṣu, with like-minded companions—whether one, two, or many—speaking in concert and holding the same views, seeks to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha."
When the bhikṣus were admonishing him, those bhikṣus who were in agreement with him said:
"Venerable sirs!
Do not speak of this bhikṣu’s good or bad qualities."
Why is this? Because these bhikṣus speak according to the Dharma and speak according to the Vinaya; whatever matters these bhikṣus have spoken, seen, and accepted, we also wish to accept.
"This bhikṣu speaks with knowledge; he does not speak without knowledge.
The bhikṣus should then admonish him, saying:
"Venerable one!..."
Do not speak these words:
"This is a monk who speaks according to the Dharma, a monk who speaks according to the Vinaya. Why is that?
These monks speak what is contrary to the Dharma; these monks speak according to the Vinaya.
Venerable Elders!
Do not assist in the schism of the Saṃgha; you should joyfully assist in the reconciliation of the Saṃgha.

Why is this? Because the Saṃgha is harmonious, joyful, and free from dispute; they train together as one, like water mixed with milk, illuminating through the Dharma and dwelling in peace and happiness.
"If, upon being thus admonished, he relinquishes it, that is well;
if he does not relinquish it, he should be admonished a second and a third time. If he relinquishes this matter, that is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
"If a bhikṣu, being obstinate and contrary, when other bhikṣus are instructing him in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya within the common teachings, should obstinately say to himself:
'Venerable sirs!'"
"You must not speak to me of good or evil matters,
nor shall I speak to you of good or evil matters.
The bhikṣus should then admonish him, saying:

"Elder! When the bhikṣus instruct one another according to the Dharma and the Vinaya within the common teachings, you must not refuse to accept it; you, too, should instruct the bhikṣus according to the Dharma and the Vinaya."
Why is this? Because the assembly of the Tathāgata’s disciples instruct one another and admonish one another in turn, thereby emerging together from faults, and thus wholesome dharmas increase.
"If, upon being thus admonished, he relinquishes [the matter], it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, he should be admonished a second and a third time. If he relinquishes the matter, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."

"If a bhikṣu, residing in dependence upon a town or village, defiles families and engages in evil conduct—such that his defiling of families is both seen and heard of, and his engagement in evil conduct is both seen and heard of."
The bhikṣus should admonish them, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
You have defiled families and committed evil deeds; that you have defiled families has been seen and heard, and that you have committed evil deeds has also been seen and heard."
"You all, get out; you should not remain here.
Those bhikṣus said, "The Saṃgha acts out of favoritism, out of hatred, out of fear, and out of delusion."
Why is this? Because there are bhikṣus who have committed such identical offenses, yet some are expelled while others are not.
The bhikṣus should then admonish him, saying:
"Elder! Do not speak thus:
'The Saṃgha follows favoritism, follows hatred, follows fear, and follows delusion.'"
"There are bhikṣus who have committed the same offense, yet some are expelled while others are not.
Why is this? Because the Saṃgha does not follow favoritism, does not follow hatred, does not follow fear, and does not follow delusion."
"Elders!
You defile families and engage in evil conduct; you are seen and heard to defile families, and you are seen and heard to engage in evil conduct.
Depart from here; do not dwell among us."
"If, upon being thus admonished, he relinquishes [the matter], it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, he should be admonished a second and a third time. If he relinquishes that matter, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
"Venerable sirs!
Regarding the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas— nine of which are offenses at the first instance and four of which require up to three admonitions—
if a bhikṣu commits any one of these offenses, he should be granted *parivāsa* according to the duration for which he knowingly concealed it."
After the parivāsa has been completed, one should undergo the mānatva for six days and six nights within the Saṃgha.
Once the mānatva has been performed, one should be rehabilitated from the offense before a community of twenty monks.
If there is one person missing such that the number does not reach twenty, this bhikṣu cannot be cleared of his offense, and the other bhikṣus should be rebuked; such is the nature of the Dharma.
Now I ask the Venerable Ones: [Is it so?]
Is it pure in this regard?
Is it pure in this regard?
Is it pure in this regard?
“Venerable sirs!
Since there is silence, you are pure in this matter; thus shall this be held.
The thirteen matters are concluded. “Venerable sirs!”
These two indeterminate rules (*aniyata-dharma*) are recited every half-month during the *Prātimokṣa*.

"If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in a secluded, concealed place suitable for sexual intercourse, and a trustworthy laywoman (*upāsikā*) reports it according to the Dharma through one of three categories—whether as a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*—[the bhikṣu] shall be dealt with accordingly."
If a bhikṣu says of himself,

"I sat in this place," he should be dealt with according to the Dharma for each of the three categories of offenses— whether it be a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika— and that bhikṣu should be disciplined according to the Dharma as stated by a trustworthy upāsikā.
This is the first *aniyata* (undetermined) rule:

"If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in a secluded, exposed place that is not suitable for sexual intercourse, and a trustworthy *upāsikā* reports it according to the Dharma as one of two dharmas—either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*."
If a bhikṣu says of himself,

"I sat in this place," he should be dealt with according to the Dharma for each of the two categories of offenses— whether it be a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*. He should be disciplined according to the Dharma as stated by a trustworthy *upāsikā*.
"These are the two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharmas). Venerable sirs!
The two indeterminate rules have been recited."
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Is there purity in this matter?
Is there purity in this matter?
"Is there purity in this matter? "Venerable sirs!
There is purity in this matter; because you are silent, it shall be held as such."
The two *aniyata* rules are concluded. "Venerable sirs!
These thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited in succession every half-month as part of the *Prātimokṣa*."

"If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, should obtain an extra robe and keep it for ten days; if he keeps it longer than that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

"If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having relinquished the kaṭhina privileges, should stay overnight apart from any one of his three robes in another location—except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha—he commits an offense of niḥsargika-pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, should obtain an out-of-season robe, and if that bhikṣu requires it, he should take it and quickly have it made into a robe for use."
If it is insufficient and there is a source from which more may be expected, one is permitted to keep it for one month in order to fulfill it.
If this period is exceeded—whether the item is sufficient or insufficient—it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat an old robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu asks for a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, except at the appropriate time, it is an offense of forfeiture and expiation (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
The 'appropriate time' refers to the occasion when one's robes have been lost."

"If a bhikṣu has lost his robes, he may beg for robes from a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative; if they offer them of their own accord, he may accept a set of upper and lower robes."
If one accepts more than this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a householder or a householder’s wife provides the price for a robe for a bhikṣu, saying:
'I have prepared the price for such a robe; buy such a robe and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu.'"
"Before being invited, this bhikṣu, for the sake of something fine, went there and urged him, saying:
'Excellent, householder!
Purchase such a garment of such a color with this price of cloth and give it to me.'"
If he obtains the robe, it is an *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a monk, when a householder and a housewife have each prepared the price for such a robe, saying:
'We have prepared the price for such a robe to buy such a robe and give it to a certain monk'..."
"Without having been previously invited, this bhikṣu, for the sake of something fine, goes to them and urges them, saying:
'Excellent, householder!
Each of you should prepare the price for such a robe; together, let us make one robe of such a color and give it to me.'"
If he obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"For the sake of a bhikṣu, if a king or a high minister sends a messenger with the value of a robe to be given to that bhikṣu, and the messenger arrives and says:
'This value for a robe has been sent by the king or the high minister; Venerable Sir, you should accept it.'"
The bhikṣu said:
"I may not accept this price for the robe; one should accept it only when a pure robe has been brought.
The messenger said:
"Does the Venerable One have an attendant?
If a bhikṣu requires robes, he should point out an attendant—whether a monastery worker or a lay follower (upāsaka)—and say:
"This person can serve as an attendant for the bhikṣu."
The messenger arrives and exhorts him, saying:
"Excellent, steward!
With this price for robes, purchase such pure robes and give them to the bhikṣu so-and-so; when that bhikṣu comes to receive the robes, then give them to him."
Having exhorted him thus, the messenger returned to where the bhikṣu was and said, "I have already exhorted the attendant you indicated, O Venerable One; when you require robes, go and take them."
“If a bhikṣu requires robes, he should go to the attendant and say:
‘I need robes! I need robes!’”
The second and third times he should speak in the same manner.
If he obtains the robe, it is well; if he does not obtain it, he should stand silently before the official for a fourth, fifth, and sixth time. If he obtains the robe, it is well;
if he does not obtain it, and he seeks it beyond this limit and obtains a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If he does not obtain it, he should go to where the value of the robe was sent from, either going himself or sending a messenger, saying:

"You were sent to deliver the value of a robe for a certain bhikṣu; that bhikṣu has not received the value of the robe from you at all. You yourself must take care of it and ensure it is not lost; such is the rule."
Regarding the ten matters: "If a bhikṣu makes a new matting of pure black sheep’s wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu makes a new matting, he should use two parts of pure black sheep’s wool, three parts of white, and four parts of inferior [wool]."
If it exceeds the proper measure, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding using a mixture of *kauśeya* silk and pure black sheep’s wool, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu makes a new mat, he must use it for six years.

If he makes a new mat before six years have passed—whether or not he has disposed of his old mat—except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (saṃgha-kamma), it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika)."
"If a bhikṣu makes a new rug or sitting mat (niṣīdana), he must attach a piece from an old rug measuring one Sugata-span on each side, in order to spoil its color."
If one does not [dispose of the old one] and makes a new bedding, woolen rug, or *niṣīdana*, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, while traveling on a road, obtains wool and needs it, he may take it for up to three *yojanas*."
If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, with his own hand, takes up raw gold or silver, or causes another to take it up, lift it, or process it for attachment [to goods], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of trade involving raw materials or processed goods, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
[The twentieth section ends. "If a bhikṣu obtains an extra bowl, he may keep it for ten days."
If he exceeds this limit, it is an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, whose bowl has fewer than five patches, begs for a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, it is an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
This bowl should be relinquished within the assembly.
It should be given to the one with the lowest-ranking bowl in the assembly, saying these words:
"Venerable sir!..."
"This bowl is to be received and maintained; it shall be discontinued only when it breaks.
This is the natural law of the matter.
"If a bhikṣu is ill and ought to consume ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, fresh butter, or fat, he may receive them once and consume them for seven days."
If, after seven days have passed, one consumes what remains without relinquishing it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu, having given a robe to another bhikṣu, later becomes angry and displeased, and either takes it back himself or causes another to take it back, [the one] who obtains the robe commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣu, when one month of the spring season remains, seeks a rain-bathing robe, he must have it finished and accept its use when half a month remains.
If he has not yet reached the time for seeking the rain-bathing robe, yet finishes it and accepts its use, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣu himself begs for thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it into a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a householder or a housewife has a weaver weave a robe for a bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu, having not been previously invited, goes there for the sake of excellence and encourages the weaver, saying:
'Excellent, householder!'"
"If this robe is being made for me, you should weave it well so that it is fine, long, and wide; I shall give you the price for it, or the price for food.
If, having been thus enticed, she obtains the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu obtains an urgent gift of robes ten days before the *pravāraṇā*, he may, if he requires it, accept and keep it until the time of the *pravāraṇā*.
If he keeps it beyond that time, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

"When the three months of summer have not yet arrived, if a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya during the final month of summer has a cause for apprehension or fear, he may leave one or another of his three robes with a layperson and remain apart from it for up to six nights."
If one exceeds [the limit], except by formal authorization from the Saṃgha (saṃgha-kamma), it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object is intended for the Saṃgha, diverts it to himself, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."
The thirty matters are concluded. "Venerable sirs!
The thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas have been recited.
Now I ask the venerable sirs:"
Is it pure in this regard?
Is it pure in this regard?
Is it pure in this regard?
"Venerable sirs!
Since there is silence, you are pure in this matter; thus shall this be held.
Venerable sirs!"
These ninety-two *pāyattika* rules are recited in succession every half-month during the *Prātimokṣa*.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing the truth, deliberately speaks a falsehood, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu speaks of someone’s lineage or physical appearance, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu engages in divisive speech, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu knows that a dispute has been settled by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, yet he initiates it again, saying:..."
"If one says, 'This *karmavācanā* is not concluded;
it shall be performed again,' and acts upon these same conditions without change, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, except when a man of intelligence is present, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu teaches the dharma in phrases to one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, for his own sake, claims before one who has not received full ordination that he has attained a superhuman state, saying:
'I know thus; I see thus.'"
To speak of what is real [when it is not] constitutes a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu, knowing of a bhikṣu’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (*saṃghakamma*), it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha is about to distribute property, first consents to its being given and later objects, saying:
'Venerable sir!
Out of a sense of intimacy, you have diverted the property of the Saṃgha to another person.'"
“[This constitutes] a pāyattika.
‘If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha recites the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month, should say:
“Venerable sir!...”’”
"What is the use of reciting these minor precepts?
They cause the bhikṣus to give rise to doubt and regret.
To disparage the precepts with such words, for reasons no different from those previously mentioned, constitutes a pāyattika offense.
The ten matters are concluded: "If a bhikṣu destroys seeds or ruins a 'village of spirits' (a grove), it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu annoys another with evasive speech, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu speaks with reproach, it is a pāyattika.

"If a bhikṣu, in an open space within a monastic dwelling, spreads out a bed, a chair, a mat, or a pillow—whether he spreads them himself or causes another to spread them—and when departing does not pick them up himself nor cause another to pick them up, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣu spreads out bedding or mats within a monastery cell—whether he spreads them himself or has another spread them—and upon departing does not remove them himself nor have another remove them, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and resentment, drags a bhikṣu out from within a monastic dwelling—whether he does so himself or causes another to do so—even down to saying: 'Get out!'"

Pāyattika. "If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has already spread out bedding within a monastic dwelling, comes later and spreads his own bedding with the intent to cause disturbance and make him leave, and does so for no other reason, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu spreads a bed with pointed legs on an upper story of a monastic dwelling and sits or lies upon it, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living organisms, pours it onto grass or mud, or causes another to pour it, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣu undertakes the construction of a large dwelling and provides it with doors and windows, he should have it covered two or three times at most; he must instruct that it be situated on a plot of land with sparse grass.
If he exceeds this, it is a pāyattika."
The twentieth section concludes: "If a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣuṇī without having been appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu, though appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct a bhikṣuṇī, does so from sunset until the appearance of the dawn light, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu goes to the dwelling place of bhikṣuṇīs to give instruction without having informed a virtuous bhikṣu, except at other times, it is a pāyattika.
'Other times' refers to the time of illness."
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'Venerable sir!
You instruct the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food.'"
“...a pāyattika. ‘If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place together with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.

‘If a bhikṣu makes an appointment to travel on a road together with a bhikṣuṇī, even as far as between villages, except when there is suspicion or fear regarding traveling with caravan merchants, it is a pāyattika.’”
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel together by boat, whether upstream or downstream—except for a direct crossing—it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative—except in exchange for trade—it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a bhikṣuṇī has praised [the meal], eats [the food], except in the case of an established donor (pūrvaka-dāyaka), it is a pāyattika."
The thirty rules are concluded: "If a bhikṣu, at a place where a single meal is offered, eats more than one meal when not ill, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu eats from place to place, except during times of illness or times of [receiving] robes, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, having finished eating and left his seat, eats food that has not been made into *vighasa* (leftover food), it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has finished eating and left his seat, and that the latter has not made the food into *vighasa*, should urge him out of a desire to annoy him, saying:
'Venerable sir!'"
"Eat this food.
If he eats it, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu places in his mouth that which has not been given and not received—except for water and tooth-sticks—it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu eats stored food, it is a pāyattika.

"If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson where cakes and parched grain are being freely offered, he may accept two or three bowls and, having gone outside, eat them together with bhikṣus who are not ill."
If one accepts food that is not shared in excess, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, when not ill, begs for himself ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, curdled milk, fish, or meat—thus begging for choice foods and eating them—it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu eats apart from the community, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika.
The 'appropriate times' are: when one is ill, when it is the time for robes, when traveling, when on a boat, during a great assembly, and when non-Buddhists offer food."

The forty rules are concluded: "If a bhikṣu, being without illness, for his own sake burns grass, wood, or cow dung—whether he burns them himself or causes another to burn them—with the exception of a specific cause, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu stays in the same room with a person who has not received full ordination for more than three nights, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, having already given his consent (*karmakāmatā*) to a formal act (*karman*), later becomes resentful and displeased, saying:
'I did not give my consent; I gave it unwillingly; this *karman* is not valid; I do not give this consent.'"
[Pāyattika. "If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'Venerable sir!'"
"Come with me into the village; when we arrive there, I shall give you food—either giving it to you myself or having someone else give it.
Later, wishing to drive him away, he then said: "Go!"
"I do not delight in dwelling with you; I delight in dwelling alone.
If one creates such a cause and condition without deviation, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu speaks these words:"
"Venerable one!
I know that the Blessed One has declared these things to be obstructive dharmas, yet you say, 'By practicing these dharmas, one cannot be obstructed from the Path.
The bhikṣus should admonish him, saying:"
"Elder! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One!
It is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One; the Blessed One would never speak such words."
“The World-Honored One has declared that the dharmas which obstruct the path truly do obstruct the path.
You must abandon this evil course.
If, when thus admonished, he persists and does not abandon it, he should be admonished a second and a third time; if he abandons it, that is well.
If he does not relinquish it, the Saṃgha should perform the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*).
This bhikṣu commits a *pāyattika* offense.

"If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has evil views and does not relinquish them, and the Saṃgha has performed the formal act of suspension against him in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya..."
If one has not performed the ritual of eating together and living under the same roof according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a śrāmaṇera says:
'The Tathāgata said that sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path; I know that practicing sexual desire cannot obstruct the Path.'"
The bhikṣus should admonish him, saying:
"You, śrāmaṇera, must not slander the Blessed One!
To slander the Blessed One is unwholesome; the Blessed One does not speak such words."
“The World-Honored One has declared that sexual desire is truly an obstacle to the Path.
You must abandon this evil view.
If, when thus admonished, he persists and does not abandon it, he should be admonished a second and a third time; if he abandons it, that is well.
If they do not relinquish [the view], they should be expelled, saying:
"From this day forward, you must no longer say:
'The Buddha is my teacher.'"
"Furthermore, you must not stay together with a bhikṣu for more than three nights.
Depart; you may not remain here.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that a śrāmaṇera has not abandoned evil views and has not been expelled according to the Dharma, yet entices him back, keeps him as a follower, eats with him, or dwells with him, it is a pāyattika offense.
“If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he must apply one of three kinds of discoloration— either blue, black, or madder—
if he uses it without applying a discoloration, it is a pāyattika.”

"If a bhikṣu, within the boundaries of a monastic residence, takes for himself or causes another to take precious objects or what is considered precious, except in the case of taking them from within [the residence] to give to one who comes seeking them as their owner, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu bathes less than once every half-month, except during the special times, it is a pāyattika.
The special times are the last month and a half of spring and the first month of summer."
These two and a half months are the period of heat, the period of illness, the period of wind, the period of rain, the period of work, and the period of travel.
The fifty matters are concluded. "If a bhikṣu knowingly drinks water containing insects, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hands to a naked renunciant, male or female, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu sits in a place of sexual intimacy at a house where a meal is being served, knowing it to be so, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place at a house where food is being served, knowing it to be such, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu watches an army on its march, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu, having a legitimate reason, stays within an army for three nights, if he exceeds this, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, having a legitimate reason, stays within an army for three nights, if he watches the army set out, or views their battle standards and military formations, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, brandishes his palm as a weapon toward another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu conceals a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) known to him by another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
The sixty matters are concluded. “If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu intentionally causes another bhikṣu to give rise to doubt or regret, such that he is unhappy for even a moment, and acts with this motive without any other cause, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu has given a robe as a pure gift (niḥśraya-dāna) to one of the five groups, and subsequently uses it without relinquishing his claim, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, out of playful mockery, hides a bhikṣu’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case, or causes another to hide them, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu terrifies a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu plays in the water, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu points his finger at another, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel together on a road, even as far as a village, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place alone with a woman, it is a pāyattika."
The seventy matters are concluded: "If a bhikṣu, knowing that a person is less than twenty years of age, confers full ordination upon them, this person is not said to have received full ordination."
“Monks, you should be rebuked; this is a pāyattika offense.
If a monk, knowing that a group of thieves has planned to travel together with him on the road, even as far as a village, he commits a pāyattika offense.”
"If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hand, or causes another to dig it, or instructs by saying,
'Dig this ground,' it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu accepts a special invitation for four months, he may accept it;
if he accepts beyond that, it is a pāyattika,
except in the case of a renewed invitation or a long-term invitation.”
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'Venerable sir!
You should train yourself; do not commit the five classes of offenses.'"
The bhikṣu said: "I will not follow your words;
if I see another elder who is learned, a holder of the Dharma with deep understanding, I shall consult him, and whatever he says, I shall accept and practice."
"Except at other times, it is a pāyattika.
Other times are when a bhikṣu wishes to obtain the benefit of the Dharma and should study it, or should ask other bhikṣus about it.
If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, for every swallow, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu treats another bhikṣu with contempt, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, while the bhikṣus are engaged in a dispute, stands by in silence to listen, thinking, 'I shall remember what they say,' and acts for that reason and no other, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha is conducting formal business, departs without having given his consent (*chanda*) and without informing [the assembly], it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu dwelling in a forest hermitage enters a village at an improper time without informing a virtuous bhikṣu, except in cases of urgent necessity, it is a *pāyattika*. This concludes the eighty rules. If a bhikṣu, in a communal dining hall, goes to another place before or after a meal without informing a virtuous bhikṣu, except during the time for robes, it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣu enters the royal palace while the queen has not yet put away her treasures, even if he merely crosses the threshold, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu makes a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn, having broken [the material], it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu makes a bedstead leg, it should be no higher than eight finger-breadths of the Buddha’s measure, excluding the part inserted into the frame.
If it exceeds this, he must cut it down; it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu sits or lies upon a mattress stuffed with *tūla* cotton or *kṣauma* silk, having used it, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu makes a *niṣīdana*, he should make it according to the prescribed measure:
two *vitastis* of the Sugata in length, one and a half *vitastis* in width, with an additional *vitasti*. "
If it exceeds [the prescribed measure], having cut it down, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu makes a wound-covering cloth, it should be four Sugata-span long and two spans wide."
If it exceeds this, having cut it down, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bath robe, it should be six Sugata-spans in length and two and a half spans in width."
If it exceeds [the prescribed measure], having cut it down, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in size to the robe of the Tathāgata,
and if it exceeds [that measure], having cut it down, it is a *pāyattika*."
The robe of the Tathāgata is nine Sugata-span long and six spans wide.
"If a bhikṣu, out of malice and displeasure, slanders another with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object intended for the Saṃgha diverts it to another person, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha is reciting the Prātimokṣa Sūtra during the fortnightly assembly, speaks thus:
'Venerable sirs!'"
"I have only now learned that this dharma enters into the Sūtras and is taught within the fortnightly *Prātimokṣa*.
The monks knew that this monk had previously sat for two or three recitations of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, let alone many more!
That bhikṣu is not without offense simply because he did not know.
According to each specific offense committed, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma and should be rebuked, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."

You have lost a great benefit: when the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* was recited every half-month, you did not show respect, you were not single-minded in thought, and you did not listen to the Dharma with attentive ears.
"Having rebuked him thus, it is a pāyattika.
The ninety-two matters are concluded. "Venerable sirs!
The ninety-two pāyattika dharmas have been recited."
Now I ask the Venerable Ones:
Is there purity in this matter?
Is there purity in this matter?
"Is there purity in this matter? "Venerable sirs!
There is purity in this matter, for we are silent; thus shall this matter be upheld."
“Venerable sirs!
These four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas are recited every half-month in the sequence of the *prātimokṣa*.

‘If a bhikṣu dwelling in a forest hermitage, not having been previously informed and being without illness, receives food from outside and consumes it within, whether by chewing or eating, he should confess his transgression before another bhikṣu, saying:’”
"Venerable One! I have fallen into a blameworthy state.
I confess this transgression."

“If a bhikṣu, not being ill, accepts food from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative while inside a layperson’s house, and then eats or consumes it, he should confess his transgression to another bhikṣu, saying:
‘Venerable sir!’”
"I have fallen into a blameworthy state;
I repent for this offense.
"If a bhikṣu, having accepted an invitation to a meal at a layperson's home, has a bhikṣuṇī standing before him, pointing and saying:"
"Give rice to this bhikṣu; give soup, or fish, or meat to this bhikṣu.
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister, wait a moment!"
"Wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating.
If not even one bhikṣu rebukes them, those bhikṣus should confess their transgression to other bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma;
I repent of this dharma.

"If there is a family under the *śikṣādattaka* status, and the Saṃgha has performed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* upon them, and a bhikṣu goes there uninvited and receives food with his own hands, whether he chews it or eats it, that bhikṣu should confess to another bhikṣu, saying:"
"Elder! I have fallen into a blameworthy state.
I repent for this offense."
"Venerable sirs! The four *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas have been recited.
Now I ask the venerable sirs:"
Is there purity herein?
Is there purity herein?
Is there purity herein?
"Venerable sirs!
Since you are silent, it is clear that you are pure in this matter;
thus shall this be held. Venerable sirs!"
These are the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharmas), which are recited every half-month during the Prātimokṣa.
"One should train in wearing the inner robe neatly.
One should train in wearing the upper robe neatly."
"One should train oneself to enter a house well-covered.
One should train oneself to enter a house looking attentively.
One should train oneself to enter a house with a low voice."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house while laughing.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house with my head covered.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house with my robe tucked up behind.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house walking on my toes.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house with hands on hips.
[These are] ten matters. One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house swaying the body.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house shaking my head.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter a house swinging my arms.
One should train oneself: 'I shall sit with my body well-covered within a house.'"
"One should train oneself: 'When sitting within a house, one should look attentively.
One should train oneself: 'When sitting within a house, one should speak in a low voice.
One should train oneself: 'When sitting within a house, one should not laugh.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit inside a house with my head covered.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit inside a house with my robe tucked over both shoulders.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit inside a house with my knees drawn up.'"
Twenty Matters: "One should train oneself not to sit with legs crossed inside a house.
One should train oneself not to sit with hands on the hips inside a house.
One should train oneself not to sit inside a house while moving one's hands or feet."
"One should train oneself to receive food with a single mind.
One should train oneself to eat soup and rice in equal measure.
One should train oneself not to scoop out food from one side."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not eat stuffing my cheeks.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not eat sticking out my tongue.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not take mouthfuls of food that are too large.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not open my mouth wide in expectation of food.
One should train oneself in thirty matters: 'I shall not pick at my food into balls.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not bite off half a morsel.'"
"One should train oneself not to speak while eating.
One should train oneself not to wipe the bowl with one's finger while eating.
One should train oneself not to lick the hands while eating."
"One should train oneself not to eat while sucking on one's fingers.
One should train oneself not to eat while making smacking sounds.
One should train oneself not to eat while making slurping sounds."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not eat by stuffing my mouth.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not let rice fall while eating.
(Fortieth item) One should train oneself: 'I shall not shake my hand while eating.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One shall not look at the bowl of a fellow monk with a mind of disdain.
One should train oneself: 'One shall look upon one's own bowl with a composed mind.
One should train oneself: 'Unless one is ill, one shall not request food for oneself.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One shall not cover the soup with rice and then expect to receive more.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not receive a vessel for rice with greasy hands.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not discard leftover food from one's bowl onto the ground.'"
"One who is standing should not preach the Dharma to one who is sitting, except when ill; this is a training to be observed.
One who is sitting should not preach the Dharma to one who is lying down, except when ill; this is a training to be observed."
"One should train oneself: 'When one is seated on a lower seat, one shall not preach the Dharma to a person seated on a high bed, except in the case of illness.
(Fifty matters) One should train oneself: 'One shall not preach the Dharma to a person wearing leather sandals, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one wearing wooden clogs, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one with their head covered, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Unless one is ill, I shall not preach the Dharma to a person with their head wrapped;
unless one is ill, I shall not preach the Dharma to a person squatting with knees drawn up.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not teach the Dharma to one who is sitting with legs crossed, except when ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not teach the Dharma to one who is holding a knife, except when ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except when one is ill, I shall not preach the Dharma to those carrying bows and arrows.
One should train oneself: 'Except when one is ill, I shall not preach the Dharma to those carrying staffs.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to one who is holding a sunshade.
This is one of the sixty matters. One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to one who is behind me while I am in front. This is another."
"One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not teach the Dharma to one who is mounted on a vehicle.
One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not teach the Dharma to one on the road while I am off the road.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except when ill, I shall not void excrement, urine, mucus, or saliva upon living grass.
One should train oneself: 'Except when ill, I shall not void excrement, urine, mucus, or saliva into water.'"
"One should not stand while defecating or urinating, except when ill; this is how one should train.
The sixty-six rules of training for the community are concluded. "Venerable sirs!
The rules of training for the community have been recited."
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Is there purity in this matter?
Is there purity in this matter?
"Is there purity herein? "Venerable sirs!
There is purity herein, for we are silent; thus shall this matter be held."
"Venerable sirs!
These seven principles for settling disputes are recited every half-month as part of the Prātimokṣa.
If a case is appropriate for settlement in the presence of the person concerned, one should grant that person the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence)."
"To one who should be granted the *smṛtivinaya*, grant the *smṛtivinaya*.
To one who should be granted the *amūḍhavinaya*, grant the *amūḍhavinaya*."
"To those who should be granted the *pratijñākāraka-vinaya*, grant the *pratijñākāraka-vinaya*.
To those who should be granted the *tatsvabhāva-śuddha-vinaya*, grant the *tatsvabhāva-śuddha-vinaya*."
"To one who should be dealt with according to the *yebhuyyasika* (majority decision) *kamma*, the *yebhuyyasika kamma* should be administered.

To one who should be dealt with according to the *tassapāpiyasika* (further penalty) *kamma*, the *tassapāpiyasika kamma* should be administered. To one who should be dealt with according to the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass) *kamma*, the *tiṇavatthāraka kamma* should be administered."
"Venerable sirs! The seven methods for settling disputes have already been recited.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: [Are you pure in this matter?]"
Is it pure in this regard?
Is it pure in this regard?
Is it pure in this regard?
“Venerable sirs!
Since there is silence, you are pure in this matter; let it be held thus.
The seven methods for settling disputes are concluded. “Venerable sirs!”
These are the conforming dharmas; every half-month, the Prātimokṣa is recited in succession.
As for "conforming to the two divisions of the Vinaya," it means conforming to the practice of these dharmas.
"Venerable sirs! The dharmas that accord with the training have been recited.
Now I ask the venerable sirs: [Are you pure in this matter?]"
Is it pure in this regard?
Is it pure in this regard?
Is it pure in this regard?
"Venerable sirs!
Since you are silent, it is clear that you are pure in this matter;
thus shall this be held. Venerable sirs!"

Having already explained the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, having explained the four *pārājika* rules, having explained the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, having explained the two *aniyata* rules, having explained the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, having explained the ninety-two *pāyattika* rules, having explained the four *prātideśanīya* rules, having explained the *śaikṣa* rules, and having explained the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* rules, this is called the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. It is contained within the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra*; these are the rules of conformity to the Dharma, which all students must not transgress.
The Buddha said:
"Vipaśyin Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the Saṅgha of those who have attained tranquility, briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
'Patience is the supreme path; Nirvāṇa is declared by the Buddha to be the highest.'"
"One who causes affliction to others while claiming to have left the household life is not called a śramaṇa.
"Śikhin Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the Saṅgha of tranquility, briefly recited the Prātimokṣa:
"Just as a person with clear vision Is able to avoid dangerous and evil paths;
"In this world there are wise people who are able to distance themselves from all evils.
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin, for the sake of the peaceful Saṅgha, briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
'Do not harm others, do not speak ill; act in accordance with what is taught in the precepts.'"
"Know moderation in eating; always delight in dwelling in seclusion;
with a pure mind, delight in diligence—this is called the teaching of all Buddhas.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda Buddha, for the sake of the silent Saṅgha, briefly recited the Prātimokṣa:
"Just as a bee gathers from a flower, taking its nectar without destroying its color or fragrance;
so too, one should not disrupt another's affairs, nor observe what they have done or left undone."
"Observe your own conduct alone, and examine closely what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Konāgamana Buddha, for the sake of the Saṅgha of tranquility, briefly recited the Prātimokṣa:
'If you wish to attain a virtuous mind, do not be negligent; You should diligently train in the wholesome dharmas of the Noble Ones.'"
"If there is one who knows how to dwell in the stillness of a single mind, then they shall no longer have sorrow or affliction.
"Kāśyapa Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of the silent Saṅgha, briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
'Commit no evil whatsoever; one should fully cultivate wholesome dharmas.'"
"Purify your own mind; this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, for the sake of the Saṅgha of the Peaceful, briefly recited the Prātimokṣa:
'To guard the body is excellent!'"
It is good to guard the mouth;
it is excellent to guard the mind;
it is good to guard all [the sense faculties].
The bhikṣu who guards all [the senses] shall be freed from all suffering;
the bhikṣu who restrains speech and mind and does not commit evil with the body—
these three paths of action being pure— he attains the path attained by the noble ones.
If one is struck or reviled and does not retaliate, if one harbors no resentment toward those who feel hatred,
and maintains a mind always pure amidst those who are angry, one will see others committing evil but refrain from doing so oneself.
The Seven Buddhas, as World-Honored Ones, were able to rescue and protect the world;
the precept sūtra they spoke, I have now fully expounded.
All Buddhas and their disciples revere this precept sūtra.
"Having paid respect to the Sūtra of the Prātimokṣa, May you each show mutual respect.
Being fully endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, You shall be able to attain the unconditioned path.
Thus concludes the recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
The Saṃgha attains the *poṣadha* through a single mind.
The *Mahāsāṃghika* precepts state: “Maintaining the precepts purifies body and speech; Restraining the mind and maintaining right mindfulness;
Extensive learning gives rise to true wisdom— All this has the precepts as its foundation.”
Precepts are a wondrous treasury of jewels, and they are also the seven riches;
precepts are a great navigator, able to ferry one across the ocean of birth and death;
precepts are a pool of cool clarity, for bathing away all afflictions.
Precepts are the art of fearlessness, extinguishing and subduing the harm of perverse poisons.
Precepts are the ultimate companion, able to cross perilous and evil paths.
Precepts are the gate to the nectar of immortality, the path by which all the sages have gone.
Holding the precepts with an unshakable mind, Dedicated and free from negligence;
Not violating the characteristics of right precepts, Nor harboring a mind of wrong livelihood—
This is called pure morality, Praised by all Buddhas.
"Therefore, with joy, one upholds the pure body of precepts.
— *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya Bhikṣu-śīla-mūla* (The Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya: Bhikṣu Precept Manual)
